introduction: Rome celebrates Caesar's triumph, but his growing authority troubles men who fear that the republic is yielding to a single ruler. Cassius works on the honorable Brutus, whose friendship with Caesar conflicts with his sense of public duty. Omens, private appeals, and competing accounts of ambition surround a decision that its makers hope to justify as an act of freedom. Once political conviction becomes a license for violence, the ability to explain events to Rome's citizens becomes as consequential as the deed itself.

fullSynopsis.text: While Roman citizens celebrate Caesar, the tribunes Flavius and Marullus rebuke their abandonment of Pompey and remove decorations honoring the new victor. At the Lupercal festival Caesar dismisses a soothsayer's warning about the Ides of March. Cassius, resenting Caesar's elevation above his fellow Romans, probes Brutus's fear of kingship and invokes his family's defense of liberty. Casca reports that Caesar refused Antony's offer of a crown three times, though he interprets the refusals skeptically. During a violent storm Cassius recruits Casca and arranges forged letters, apparently from concerned citizens, to encourage Brutus to act.

Brutus decides that Caesar must die to prevent the possible corruption of his power, acknowledging that he has no personal grievance or proof that Caesar's reason has already yielded to passion. The letters reinforce his sense that Rome demands intervention. He joins the conspiracy but rejects both an oath and Cassius's proposal to kill Antony as well. He wants the assassination to resemble a necessary sacrifice rather than butchery. Portia presses him to share the burden of his secrets, showing a self-inflicted wound as proof of endurance, and he promises to confide in her.

Calphurnia's dream and unfavorable sacrificial signs briefly persuade Caesar to remain at home. Decius reinterprets the dream as a promise of Rome's renewal through Caesar and suggests that absence could cost him a crown or expose him to ridicule. Caesar changes his mind. Artemidorus prepares a written warning naming the conspirators, while Portia anxiously seeks news. At the Capitol Caesar postpones reading the warning. The conspirators surround him with a petition for the recall of Metellus Cimber's brother; after Caesar refuses, they stab him, Brutus among them, and proclaim liberty.

Antony secures permission to honor Caesar at the funeral, despite Cassius's concern. Brutus first persuades the citizens that Caesar's ambition made his death necessary to preserve their freedom. Antony then turns their approval into outrage. By questioning the charge of ambition, showing Caesar's wounds, and revealing gifts to the people in his will, he makes the assassination seem a betrayal. The crowd leaves intent on revenge, and Brutus and Cassius flee Rome. Citizens seize Cinna the poet because he shares a conspirator's name and refuse to spare him when he explains the mistake.

Antony, Octavius, and Lepidus compile death lists, even sacrificing relatives, and Antony proposes reducing Caesar's legacies. Their enemies gather armies near Sardis. Brutus and Cassius quarrel over bribery, discipline, money, and the strains on their friendship, then reconcile. Brutus discloses that Portia has killed herself; reports also bring news of the triumvirs' executions, including Cicero's. Against Cassius's preference to wait, Brutus persuades him to march to Philippi before the enemy grows stronger. That night Caesar's ghost appears to Brutus, promising another meeting at Philippi.

At Philippi, Brutus gains an initial advantage over Octavius, but Antony defeats Cassius's forces. Pindarus mistakenly reports Titinius captured when he is actually being welcomed by friends. Believing the battle and his friend lost, Cassius has Pindarus kill him with the sword used against Caesar. Titinius returns, discovers the error, and kills himself. Brutus continues the fighting; young Cato falls, and Lucilius protects Brutus by posing as him, earning Antony's respect. Finally defeated, Brutus persuades Strato to hold his sword and runs upon it. Antony praises him as the one conspirator moved by the common good, and Octavius orders an honorable burial and offers employment to his surviving followers.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Flavius and Marullus disperse citizens celebrating Caesar and strip his images of honors, fearing the power that popular enthusiasm is giving him. At the festival Caesar dismisses a warning about the Ides of March. Cassius appeals to Brutus's love of liberty, contrasting Caesar's human weaknesses with the supremacy he now enjoys. Brutus admits that he fears Caesar becoming king but promises only to consider Cassius's arguments. Caesar, meanwhile, recognizes Cassius as a dangerous observer. Casca reports Caesar's repeated refusal of a crown and the silencing of the tribunes. As a storm fills Rome with alarming reports, Cassius interprets the portents against Caesar, recruits Casca, and sends Cinna to place forged appeals where Brutus will find them.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Brutus reasons that Caesar may become dangerous if crowned and must be killed before that possibility develops. A planted letter seems to confirm Rome's demand for his action. He welcomes the conspirators, rejects an oath, excludes Cicero, and overrules Cassius's plan to kill Antony. Portia insists on her right to share his troubles, and he promises disclosure. Ligarius joins out of trust in Brutus. Calphurnia persuades Caesar to stay home after terrifying dreams and omens, but Decius flatters him with another interpretation and the prospect of a crown. Caesar leaves with the conspirators. Artemidorus prepares a written warning, and Portia anxiously sends Lucius for news while the soothsayer seeks another chance to speak to Caesar.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Caesar brushes aside Artemidorus's warning and enters the Capitol. A petition for Metellus's banished brother gives the conspirators an opportunity to surround and stab him. They claim to have freed Rome and bathe their hands in his blood. Antony negotiates safe access and permission to speak at the funeral; Brutus overrides Cassius's warning but forbids direct blame of the killers. Brutus's defense of Roman freedom initially wins the crowd. Antony reverses that response through irony, memories of Caesar, the sight of his wounds, and the will's gifts to the citizens. The people rush toward revenge, and Brutus and Cassius are reported fleeing. In the streets the mob turns against Cinna the poet, disregarding his denial that he is Cinna the conspirator.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Antony, Octavius, and Lepidus mark enemies and relatives for death. Antony sends for Caesar's will to reduce its financial obligations and privately dismisses Lepidus as a useful subordinate. At Sardis, Brutus and Cassius hide their quarrel from their soldiers, then argue about the punishment of bribery, Cassius's conduct, and money for Brutus's troops. They reconcile, and Brutus reveals Portia's suicide. Further reports describe the triumvirs' proscriptions and Cicero's death. Cassius wants the enemy to exhaust itself approaching them, but Brutus urges an immediate march to Philippi while their strength is at its height. Cassius yields. After his companions sleep, Brutus sees Caesar's ghost, which tells him they will meet again at Philippi.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: The opposing generals exchange accusations before battle, and Cassius voices unease about ominous birds. Brutus refuses the prospect of being led captive through Rome. His attack initially succeeds against Octavius, but Cassius's side loses to Antony. Unable to see clearly, Cassius sends Titinius to identify nearby troops. Pindarus mistakes their friendly welcome for capture, and Cassius orders him to administer a fatal sword thrust. Returning with a victory garland, Titinius discovers Cassius dead and kills himself. Brutus fights again; Cato is killed, while Lucilius impersonates Brutus and is spared by Antony. Facing defeat, Brutus dies on his own sword with Strato's assistance. Antony honors his motives, and Octavius arranges burial, welcomes his servants, and orders the victorious army to rest.
